- If water reached another floor or ceiling below: Let me know—this is more urgent for potential water damage.

Send me your address/ZIP and I’ll search for an emergency plumber who can come out right now.</action>

<action type="say">
Focus on safety and stopping the water from spreading until they arrive.

Do this now:

1) Safety and access
- Keep the restroom closed: put up a quick “Restroom Closed / Wet Floor” sign or a piece of paper on the door.
- Don’t let people walk through the water if you can avoid it (slip risk).
- Move any power strips, cords, boxes, or equipment off the floor near the wet area and unplug them.

2) Soak up standing water
- Use towels, paper towels, or a mop to soak up pooled water, starting at the doorway/edges and working toward the toilet.
- Wring towels into a bucket or into a trash can lined with a plastic bag. Don’t just push water into the hallway or other rooms.
- If you have a “wet floor” cone/sign, place it just outside the restroom.

3) Stop spread and protect other areas
- Check just outside the restroom door and any nearby rooms: if the floor is damp, dry those areas first so water doesn’t spread.
- If you notice water reaching carpet, try to blot it rather than scrub, so you don’t push water deeper in.

4) Light cleaning (only if it’s manageable)
- After you’ve removed most of the water, you can do a quick wipe of the floor around the toilet with a disinfectant or diluted bleach solution if available.
- Keep the door open for airflow; turn on the exhaust fan if there is one.

5) When to stop and just wait
- If you see water going into walls, under partitions/baseboards, or dripping into the ceiling below, stop active cleanup and just keep people out.
- Immediately tell property management if you see any bulging/sagging ceiling or active drips anywhere else.

If you tell me what you have on hand (mop, towels vs. only paper towels, any wet floor signs), I can give you an even shorter, exact “do this in order” list tailored to that.</action>

<action type="say">
Do this in order:

1) Block access
- Close the restroom door.
- Tape a piece of paper to the door that says: “Restroom Closed – Wet Floor.” That’s your temporary wet floor sign.
- If anyone tries to enter, tell them the restroom is closed due to a leak.

2) Remove standing water with towels
- Use the old towels first: lay them over the biggest puddles and step on them to soak up the water.
- Wring each towel into the bucket when it’s soaked, then reuse it.
- Keep going until there are no visible puddles, just a damp floor.

3) Mop the remaining damp areas
- Fill the bucket with clean water and a bit of your regular bathroom cleaner.
- Mop starting from the doorway and work your way toward the toilet so you’re not walking back over wet areas.
- Rinse and wring the mop frequently so you’re lifting water, not just spreading it.

4) Dry and air out
- After mopping, use a couple of drier towels to blot any spots that still look wet.
- Leave the door slightly open for airflow. Turn on the bathroom exhaust fan if there is one.

5) Check for spread
- Look just outside the restroom door and along any seams or thresholds; if you see damp spots, dry those with a towel.
- If you notice water reaching carpet, blot it gently with towels (don’t scrub it in).

6) If you see signs of bigger issues
- If you see water coming under walls, under partitions, or any sign that the ceiling below is wet or dripping, stop active cleanup and call property management back to tell them it may be affecting other areas.

When maintenance arrives, let them know:
- The toilet valve is shut off.
- You’ve soaked up and mopped the water.
- Any areas you’re worried may still be damp (e.g., along walls, at the door, or below).</action>
